AGENTAgentsVocabulary to use when developing agents (coding agents, design agents, embedded agents, etc.).

PARTPartsWhat an agent is made of.

PART-01

agent

harness + model + tools + policy. Never the model alone.

agents.md
PART-02

model

The LLM, identified by a string (claude-opus-5). Stateless: one context in, one message out.

agents.md
PART-03

harness

The code that runs the loop: builds context, calls the model, executes tools, appends results, stops.

agents.md
PART-04

tool

A named operation the model may request. The model sees its definition; the harness owns its implementation.

agents.md
PART-05

policy

Text in the system message that constrains behavior. Read, not enforced. Enforcement is permission, gate and sandbox.

agents.md
PART-06

skill

Instructions loaded into context on demand, not resident in every call.

agents.md
PART-07

workspace

What tools act on: a repo, a canvas, an app database.

agents.md

ROLERolesWho stands outside the loop.

ROLE-01

user

Who starts a turn: a person or a calling application.

agents.md
ROLE-02

operator

Who configures and deploys the agent.

agents.md

TIMETimeFrom one call to a whole session.

TIME-01

call

One request to the model.

agents.md
TIME-02

round

One call plus execution of the tool_calls it returned. Zero tool_calls for a final.

agents.md
TIME-03

turn

One user message, or one scheduled task, through to its last final: one round or many. The checks after a final belong to the same turn: when the tests fail, the harness sends the failure back and the fixing goes on in the same turn, so max_rounds and the budget cover it too (MP-60).

agents.md
TIME-04

session

Ordered turns sharing one transcript.

agents.md
TIME-05

run

One launch of the harness process (CLI invocation, cron job).

agents.md

MSGMessagesWhat the transcript holds and a call sends.

MSG-01

message

One unit of the transcript. Has a role: system, user, assistant, tool.

agents.md
MSG-02

transcript

Every message of the session so far, append-only. Includes tool_calls and tool_results.

agents.md
MSG-03

context

What surrounds a thing and gives it its meaning: the sentence around a word, the conversation around a message, the project around a file. The same words mean different things in different contexts, so the context is read first and the thing after.

For an AI model, the context is the context window: everything it reads before it answers, counted in tokens. One call sends it whole: the system message, the tool definitions, the transcript or its compacted form, the grounding. The model has nothing else: what is not in the context does not exist for it, and what falls out of it (compacted away, or left behind when a session ends) is gone unless it was written down somewhere it will be read again, a note, a file, a database.

agents.md
MSG-04

sidecar

A second payload carried beside a message, never merged into it: the untruncated tool output, file handles, timings. The request goes over the wire; the sidecar stays with the harness.

agents.md
MSG-05

memory

What outlives one context: the transcript, plus external stores (notes, a database).

agents.md
MSG-06

system

The message that holds the policy. Tool_definitions travel beside it, not in it.

agents.md
MSG-07

tool_call

Model → harness: tool name, arguments, id.

agents.md
MSG-08

tool_result

Harness → model: output or error of one tool_call, paired by id. Data, never instructions.

agents.md
MSG-09

final

An assistant message with no tool_call. It ends the turn once the checks after it pass; when a check fails, the failure goes back and another final comes later in the same turn. A final says nothing about whether the task succeeded. final is our name, not an API's (MP-60).

agents.md
MSG-10

stop_reason

Why a call ended: final, tool_call, max_tokens, refusal. These are our own names; each API spells them its way. Anthropic's stop_reason says end_turn for a final, tool_use for a tool_call, max_tokens and refusal; OpenAI's finish_reason says stop, tool_calls, length and content_filter (MP-60).

agents.md

TOOLToolsWhat the model may request, and what contains it.

TOOL-01

tool_definition

name + description + input_schema. What the model sees. The description is what makes the model pick it.

agents.md
TOOL-02

input_schema

The shape of a tool's arguments, as JSON Schema.

agents.md
TOOL-03

readonly

Observes only: view, grep, query. Declared at registration; a tool is classed by the worst its arguments allow.

agents.md
TOOL-04

mutating

Changes the workspace: edit, insert, shell.

agents.md
TOOL-05

destructive

Mutating and hard to undo: rm, drop, deploy.

agents.md
TOOL-06

permission

What the harness lets a tool touch: paths, hosts, commands. Enforced before the tool runs.

agents.md
TOOL-07

gate

User approval required before a tool runs. Default for destructive.

agents.md
TOOL-08

sandbox

The boundary that contains a tool's effects: files, network, processes.

agents.md
TOOL-09

grounding

Workspace state the harness injects into context each turn.

agents.md

LIMLimitsCaps, and what is cut to fit them.

LIM-01

max_rounds

Hard cap on rounds per turn.

agents.md
LIM-02

budget

Token, time or cost cap, scoped to a turn, run or session.

agents.md
LIM-03

truncate

Cut one tool_result to fit. The full output stays in the sidecar.

agents.md
LIM-04

compact

Replace the older part of the transcript in context with a summary. The replaced messages stay in the transcript and in the sidecar.

agents.md

FAILFailureHow a turn goes wrong.

FAIL-01

stall

Rounds continue without progress. Reading counts as progress; repeating the same call does not.

agents.md
FAIL-02

runaway

A turn stopped by max_rounds or budget.

agents.md

RECOVRecoveryWhat follows a final.

RECOV-01

check

The harness runs the tests or the linter after a final and, on a failure, sends it back to the model. It extends the turn: the turn ends at the last final, once the checks pass (MP-60).

agents.md
RECOV-02

review

One extra call asking a model to inspect the result against the task. Same model, another agent, or a human.

agents.md
RECOV-03

handoff

Agent stops and passes the task and its context to the user or to another agent.

agents.md

KINDKindsAn agent is named by its workspace.

KIND-01

coding agent

workspace = repo; tools = view, grep, edit, shell.

agents.md
KIND-02

design agent

workspace = canvas or artifact; tools = inspect, render, place, style.

agents.md
KIND-03

embedded agent

workspace = app data via the app's API; scope enforced by the app's access controls.

agents.md

TESTTestingWords for failures, and for the tests that find them.

TEST-01

Happy Path

The ideal scenario without errors.

testing.mdwikipedia
TEST-02

Smoke Tests

A small set of basic tests that verify whether the most critical parts of a system work at all. They answer one question: Does the application run without immediately breaking? If smoke tests fail, deeper testing is usually pointless. (Why "smoke"? From hardware: Power it on – if smoke comes out, something is seriously broken.)

testing.mdwikipedia
TEST-03

Edge Case

A situation at an extreme of the input – an empty list, the first or the last item, the maximum size – where code written for the usual case breaks.

testing.mdwikipedia
TEST-04

Transient Error

Temporary issues that resolve quickly.

testing.md
TEST-05

Intermittent Failure

A failure of the application that happens sometimes, unpredictably, and usually cannot be reproduced consistently. Request #1 works, request #2 fails, request #3 works again — even though nothing was changed. A test that fails this way is a flaky test.

Common causes: timing issues and race conditions, network instability, concurrency issues (threads or processes interfering), uninitialized values, hardware flakiness (bad RAM, overheating), resource limits hit sometimes (a connection pool exhausted).

Painful because it does not fail every time, logs often do not show a clear cause, and "works on my machine" happens a lot.

testing.md
TEST-06

Error Flood

Provisional: not defined yet. The author's note reads "a scenario with 75% errors", a working name kept until the author settles what it means (MP-62).

testing.md
TEST-07

Flaky Test

A test that passes and fails by turns with no change to the code or to the test. The fault is in the test (a fixed timeout, an order it relies on) or an intermittent failure under it.

testing.md
// Sometimes fetch() returns slow, causing timeout.
// Sometimes it's fast. So the test occasionally fails.
test("API returns data", async function () {
    const response = await fetch("/api/data");
    expect(response.ok).toBe(true);
});
TEST-08

Showstopper Bug

A defect so severe that it prevents the system from functioning or blocks further progress (development, testing, or release). Work cannot reasonably continue until it is fixed.

testing.md
TEST-09

Self-check

The application checks, by itself, that it is fit to work, as a car checks itself on the dashboard: one lamp per thing it needs, dark when that thing is there and works, lit when it is not. The lamps are the programs it calls, the environment variables, the folders it writes, the port, the versions, and what its own build was to produce. A lit lamp is the whole answer: the application is not fit, and the lamp names what to fix. It changes nothing: a self-check reads and reports. When every lamp is dark it says one line or nothing; when one is lit it names it and stops, before any work is half done.

It runs where there is something new to check: the last step of the build (PROJ-30), so an image that fails it is never shipped; and again as the first step of the run when the host may differ from the build, so a host that fails it does no work. One probe per lamp, each in its own strict shell, its output prefixed with the lamp's name, so the log says which one lit. Present is not enough: a probe exercises the tool the way the application will use it (a font subset must come out smaller with zopfli; a time zone the data uses must be known to the runtime), for the usual failure is a tool that is there and misconfigured.

Beside its neighbours: bin/configure makes the environment, the self-check tells whether it is as made (PROJ-02). A smoke test asks the same question from outside, by a test run now and then; the self-check is asked by the application itself, on every build or start. A health check is the probe of a running service, asked again and again; the self-check runs once.

Self-check, not self-test: a test is run against the code, by bin/test; a check is what the application does to itself and its surroundings, as a driver reads the dashboard before setting out. The command is bin/self-check, named for who checks: the application, not a tester from outside. A script named for one lamp, check-env for the environment, is one lamp of it; the self-check is the whole dashboard, and the build's last step adds the lamps of its own output, the folders it was to produce.

testing.md
# bin/build, the last step (PROJ-30)
bin/self-check

# bin/self-check: one lamp per thing, one shell each
bash -ue -o pipefail << 'EOF' 2>&1 | ts -s '[ffmpeg]'
    ffmpeg -version
EOF

bash -ue -o pipefail << 'EOF' 2>&1 | ts -s '[pyftsubset]'
    pyftsubset font.woff --text=12345 \
        --flavor=woff --with-zopfli --output-file=a
    pyftsubset font.woff --text=12345 \
        --flavor=woff --output-file=b
    test $(stat -c %s a) -ne $(stat -c %s b)
EOF

test -e build/front.d    # what the build was to produce
TEST-10

Safety net

The net under the trapeze: the act is done without it, and nobody falls on purpose, but when someone does, the net is what holds. In software, a second mechanism, independent of the first, that catches what the first lets through and limits the damage: a timeout behind a request that should return, a cap on a loop that should end, a job that puts back what a step should have put back. It is not the way things are meant to work; it is what holds when they do not.

An example: an agent is switched to the strongest model for one message, and the reply is meant to switch it back. The safety net: if the agent is still on the strongest model ten minutes after that message's reply, the app switches it back itself and says so in the log. The switch-back after the reply is the plan; the ten-minute check is the net.

Beside its neighbours: a self-check asks before the work whether the application is fit; an integrity check asks after it whether the data is still whole; a safety net sits under the work itself and acts when the first mechanism did not. A fallback is a second way to the same result; a safety net does not finish the job, it stops a miss from spreading. A good net is simple and independent, so it cannot fail for the same reason as what it guards, and it says when it caught something: every catch is a sign that the first way failed, and worth a look.

testing.md
// the plan: the reply switches the model back
// the net: ten minutes on, the app does it itself
const late = now - reply.at > 10 * MINUTE;
if (late && (agent.model === strongest)) {
    agent.model = agent.default_model;
    log.warn('safety net: switched the model back');
}

WORDDocumentsWords about words.

WORD-01

vocabulary

Which words we have/use.

doc.md
WORD-02

glossary

The words of a vocabulary, with their description and meaning.

doc.md

MAPMaps and waysWords for the shapes knowledge takes, and for the way a piece of work goes: where we are, where we came from, where we are going.

MAP-01

tree

One root, and every other node has exactly one parent, so there are no circles and exactly one path from the root to any node. Folders, an outline, an org chart, a family line.

In the agent notes: the folders of a note (agentdir, commondir, messages, roadmaps). A thread is a tree as long as each message answers one message.

A tree is a graph with rules; a taxonomy is a tree of kinds.

maps.md
MAP-02

graph

Things (nodes) and the links between them (edges), directed or not, with no rule on how they link: a node may have several parents, and links may run in circles.

The pages of this site are a graph: the README links to Rules and to Glossaries, Rules links to Glossaries, Glossaries to Agents, and Agents back to Rules. Glossaries has two parents, and three pages link in a circle; a tree allows neither.

Trees, taxonomies and ontologies are all graphs with rules added.

maps.md
MAP-03

map

A smaller picture that keeps what matters of something bigger: where things are and how they connect. "The map is not the territory": a map leaves things out on purpose. In code, a map (a dictionary) goes from keys to values, one value per key. Also a mind map, a concept map, a site map.

In the agent notes: a roadmap is a map of the way; "the terms and how they relate" below is a concept map; a glossary maps each term to its meaning.

maps.md
MAP-04

taxonomy

Sorting into kinds and kinds of kinds, each one "is a" the one above it: animal › bird › owl. Linnaeus for living things, the shelves of a library.

In the agent notes: a message is the author's or the agent's; a page is a subject file, a cover or a plan; a marker is .working or .cancelled.

A taxonomy is a tree, and the backbone of an ontology, which adds the other links.

maps.md
MAP-05

ontology

In philosophy, the study of what exists. In computing, a written map of what a field talks about, in four parts: the kinds of things (a message, a conversation, a subject file), the things themselves (your message of this morning asking for a glossary is a message), the relations between them (a conversation is made of messages; a reply answers a message) and the rules (every conversation has exactly one subject file). It is written down so that people and programs use the words the same way: RDF and OWL are the standards, Schema.org the best known on the web.

A glossary defines words one by one; an ontology also says how they connect. Written down once, a rename (workdir became subjectdir) happens in one place, and an agent can check a word against it.

maps.md
MAP-06

knowledge graph

An ontology filled with real things: not "a reply answers a message" in general, but "my reply of 09:30 answers your message of 09:17", one link for each pair that has it. What search engines and AI retrieval use.

In the agent notes: every message, subject file and plan of a note with their links; the app could build it, and it would feed an agent's context.

maps.md
MAP-07

roadmap

The whole way ahead: where we are going and in what order, not exactly when. A product roadmap is often three columns, Now / Next / Later. It changes as we learn, and it is meant to be shown, so it stays coarse: themes and stages, not tasks.

In the agent notes: an agent's plan for one conversation, roadmaps/<time>-agent-plan.md, its parts - [ ] **P1** … ticked as each is done, new ones added at the end; and the author's roadmaps in the app, lists of work across projects.

A roadmap is laid on a timeline, marked by milestones and fed by a backlog.

maps.md
MAP-08

milestone

The Roman stone by the road that said how far it was to Rome. In a project, a point that is reached or not ("Released", "Signed"); it takes no time, unlike a task. A diamond on a Gantt chart; on GitHub, a group of issues with a due date.

In the agent notes: the goal's steps in a subject file, drawn under the cover: done, now or next. The step that is now waits on the agent while it works and on the author after its reply; a step is named as it stands ("Testing" while now, "Tested" once done); the last is always "Done: nothing left, to the archive".

maps.md
MAP-09

breadcrumbs

The trail that shows where you are and how you got there, as in Hansel and Gretel; on a web page, Home › Docs › Page, each crumb a link back up.

Against roadmap and milestone: breadcrumbs look back (the way behind, from the root to here), a roadmap looks ahead (the whole way, in order), and a milestone is one stone on that way. A milestone passed is, in effect, a breadcrumb.

In the agent notes: the path agentdir › commondir › Terms, and the chain of Re: lines back to a conversation's first message.

maps.md
MAP-10

timeline

Events placed along time. In the agent notes: the change log at the end of each subject file, and the times in message names. A roadmap is laid on one.

maps.md
MAP-11

backlog

The work known but not yet planned, in no fixed order. In the agent notes: the "what is next" list of a subject file, the parts not yet on a roadmap. It feeds a roadmap.

maps.md
MAP-12

anatomy

The parts of one thing, seen whole: each part named where it sits, in the thing it belongs to. Borrowed from biology (the anatomy of a hand), it is common in computing: the anatomy of a button (a container, an icon on the left, a label beside it), of a URL (scheme, host, path, query, in that order), of a log line or of a file. Design systems give each component page an Anatomy section: the component drawn once, each part numbered in place, the names beside.

In the agent notes: a message as the app shows it, its header on top, its text, a voice comment's player with the transcript under it, a screenshot last.

A taxonomy sorts many things into kinds ("is a"); an anatomy opens one thing ("part of"). The parts taken out and set in a tree are a meronomy, which keeps what holds what but loses where each part sits: the anatomy is the picture of the whole, usually a labelled diagram.

maps.md
MAP-13

labelled diagram

A thing drawn whole, as it is seen, with a thin line (a callout, or leader line) from each part to its name. Nothing is moved and nothing is opened, so only the outside can be named. The common picture of an anatomy: a diagram of a flower in a school book, a device's parts in its manual, a component in a design system.

What is inside stays hidden; a cutaway opens it, an exploded view takes it apart.

maps.md
MAP-14

exploded view

The parts of a thing pulled apart along the lines they fit on, each in the place it goes, so that every part is seen and the order of putting them together can be read off the picture. Each part has a number; the numbers lead to a parts list (in industry, a bill of materials). An assembly sheet of flat-pack furniture is one.

It shows what a labelled diagram cannot: the parts behind other parts, and how they go together.

maps.md
MAP-15

cutaway

A thing drawn whole with part of its casing taken away, so the inside shows in its place: the gears of a clock behind its face, the rooms of a ship behind its hull. The edge of the cut is drawn, so it reads as opened, not as missing.

Unlike an exploded view nothing moves: the inside is seen where it works. Only what the cut opens is named; the outside is the labelled diagram's.

maps.md
MAP-16

legend

The key of a picture: a small box, set apart from the drawing, with a sample of each colour, line and sign and what it means. A map's legend says that a blue line is a river and a dashed red one a border; a chart's says which colour is which series. In British English also a key.

A label names one thing on the drawing itself; a caption says under the picture what the whole shows; a legend explains the marks, once, for all of them.

In the agent notes: the overview's colours (green done, orange waits on the author, the accent at work), and the two samples at the top of this page's terms map.

maps.md

NAMEStandard namesPlain public names, used in place of private ones: the same word for the same thing in every project, so a reader outside knows at once what it is. Several of one kind are numbered from 1: laptop1, laptop2, vps1, vps2.
